snippet.title: Comodità vs  leggerezza in SOTA, oggi vince il comfort
snippet.description:
Oggi vi porto con me sul Monte Leo I/CA-159, nel cuore del Cilento, per un'attivazione SOTA all'insegna della comodità. Considerato che la camminata di avvicinamento era di soli 20 minuti circa, mi sono permesso di caricare in zaino qualche comfort in più — per escursioni più lunghe e impegnative, invece, vale la pena valutare bene se il peso extra sia davvero giustificato.

🪑 Il setup di comfort: uno sgabello da campeggio Decathlon, leggero e pratico, e un leggio regolabile in altezza (che anni fa avevo comprato per imparare la chitarra!) diventato il supporto perfetto per radio e batteria.

📡 L'antenna: un dipolo multibanda 10-40m a link, in filo AWG 22 rivestito in silicone. Come "canna da pesca" ho usato una Spiderbeam da 10m sezionata per ottenere una punta meno esile, portandola a circa 5 metri. Ho stampato in 3D dei tappi (superiore e inferiore) e dei supporti per alloggiare il connettore PL, fissato con dei galletti. Lo stesso supporto, adattato con un BNC, mi permette di montare il dipolo anche sulla canna Decathlon da 5m, più leggera.

🎣 Un'idea di riciclo: grazie all'intuito di Angelo IU2VWK (IU2VWK), ho riutilizzato una bobina vuota del filamento per stampante 3D per avvolgere il cavo coassiale. Il coassiale monta già un RF choke (5+5 spire) installato lato antenna come balun 1:1.

📻 Radio: Xiegu G90

🎙️ Risultato: una ventina di QSO tra CW e SSB, su tre bande — 40, 30 e 20 metri.

Se ti piacciono le attivazioni portatili "smart" e le soluzioni fai-da-te per rendere la vita in montagna un po' più semplice, iscriviti al canale e fammi sapere nei commenti: tu quanto sei disposto a caricarti in spalla pur di avere un po' di comfort in più?

snippet.title: POTA-EXIT: Logic or Emotion? Why Are Radio Amateurs So Angry?
snippet.description:
Changes to Parks on the Air have generated plenty of heat, particularly amongst UK activators. But before we reach for the emergency exit, perhaps we should do something wonderfully unfashionable on social media:

Stop. Think. Look at the evidence.

In this video I look at the POTA debate through the lens of behavioural science. Are we making rational judgements about what has actually changed, or are loss aversion, status quo bias, group behaviour and emotion quietly operating the controls?

And perhaps there is a bigger question.

What is amateur radio actually for?

The answer isn’t defined by Facebook, YouTube, an awards programme, a national society, or indeed by how amateur radio happens to have developed in the United States.

Amateur radio is an international radiocommunication service.

The International Telecommunication Union defines the Amateur Service as being for self-training, intercommunication and technical investigations, carried out by authorised people interested in radio technique for a personal, non-commercial purpose. 

Those few words capture something rather wonderful.

We learn.

We experiment.

We communicate.

And we do it internationally.

POTA happens to provide a magnificent framework for doing all three outdoors. It encourages experimentation with antennas, propagation, portable power, radios and operating techniques. More importantly, it gets people outside and puts radio amateurs in contact with other radio amateurs across towns, countries and continents.

The IARU’s guidance on amateur operating also emphasises self-discipline and good operating practice. 

So whatever side of the present POTA discussion you’re on, I’d suggest something much more important than winning an argument:

Collaboration. Courtesy. Kindness.

Disagree with an idea without declaring war on the person proposing it. Ask questions. Share evidence. Help newcomers. Listen to people operating under different national regulations and circumstances. Remember that somebody disagreeing with you about a park reference hasn’t suddenly become your mortal enemy.

And perhaps most importantly, get on the radio.

POTA isn’t really a database, an award or a collection of reference numbers.

localized.title: POTA-EXIT: Logic or Emotion? Why Are Radio Amateurs So Angry?
localized.description:
Changes to Parks on the Air have generated plenty of heat, particularly amongst UK activators. But before we reach for the emergency exit, perhaps we should do something wonderfully unfashionable on social media:

Stop. Think. Look at the evidence.

In this video I look at the POTA debate through the lens of behavioural science. Are we making rational judgements about what has actually changed, or are loss aversion, status quo bias, group behaviour and emotion quietly operating the controls?

And perhaps there is a bigger question.

What is amateur radio actually for?

The answer isn’t defined by Facebook, YouTube, an awards programme, a national society, or indeed by how amateur radio happens to have developed in the United States.

Amateur radio is an international radiocommunication service.

The International Telecommunication Union defines the Amateur Service as being for self-training, intercommunication and technical investigations, carried out by authorised people interested in radio technique for a personal, non-commercial purpose. 

Those few words capture something rather wonderful.

We learn.

We experiment.

We communicate.

And we do it internationally.

POTA happens to provide a magnificent framework for doing all three outdoors. It encourages experimentation with antennas, propagation, portable power, radios and operating techniques. More importantly, it gets people outside and puts radio amateurs in contact with other radio amateurs across towns, countries and continents.

The IARU’s guidance on amateur operating also emphasises self-discipline and good operating practice. 

So whatever side of the present POTA discussion you’re on, I’d suggest something much more important than winning an argument:

Collaboration. Courtesy. Kindness.

Disagree with an idea without declaring war on the person proposing it. Ask questions. Share evidence. Help newcomers. Listen to people operating under different national regulations and circumstances. Remember that somebody disagreeing with you about a park reference hasn’t suddenly become your mortal enemy.

And perhaps most importantly, get on the radio.

POTA isn’t really a database, an award or a collection of reference numbers.

It’s people using radio, learning things, experimenting and talking to one another.

Which sounds remarkably close to what amateur radio was supposed to be all along.

73, Dave, G3LRC

snippet.title: Is VHF Dead? How to Upgrade to General Unlock Global HF Ham Radio.
snippet.description:
Tired of Dead Repeaters? Step Up to General Class Amateur Radio!

You passed your Technician exam, picked up a budget handheld, keyed up the local repeater, and… crickets. If you’re feeling isolated and trapped on VHF/UHF line-of-sight bands, you are experiencing Technician Burnout. But the hobby isn't broken—you’re just missing out on 90% of the spectrum!

In this deep-dive guide, we break down everything you need to know about making the ultimate jump from Technician to General Class, escaping local line-of-sight barriers, and unlocking global High Frequency (HF) communication!

Key Takeaways & Resources

snippet.title: Every contractor says they're licensed and insured. Almost nobody checks what that actually means.
snippet.description:
Every contractor says they're licensed and insured. Almost nobody
checks what that actually means.

It's three separate things, not two:

LICENSE — the state permits them to do the work
GENERAL LIABILITY — covers damage to your house
WORKERS' COMP — covers the crew if someone gets hurt

Plenty of contractors carry one and not the other. Workers' comp is
the one people miss, and it's the expensive one. If a worker is
injured on your roof and there's no comp behind him, that claim can
end up pointed at you and your homeowners policy.

A certificate the contractor hands you isn't verification. Call the
carrier listed on it, confirm the dates are current, and confirm
the insured business name matches the name on your contract.

Check all three before you sign anything. Contractor Compare pulls
license status, insurance, complaints, legal actions, and business
history from public sources and scores the risk — free, in about
30 seconds.

- Can I be named as certificate holder so I'm notified if it lapses?

A contractor in good standing won't mind any of these questions.

snippet.title: Caí no Golpe: Homem compra carro com placas clonadas e perde R$ 68 mil em São Paulo
snippet.description:
Um técnico de enfermagem buscava um carro mais novo para sua família e acabou sendo vítima de um golpe ao comprar um carro clonado. Após ver um anúncio online, a vítima negociou com um vendedor que se apresentava como Francisco. Eles acertaram um encontro em Vila Prudente, zona leste de São Paulo, onde um homem chamado Pedro, que dizia ser filho do vendedor, mostrou o veículo.

O carro, modelo 2018, estava anunciado por R$ 73.500, um valor abaixo do mercado. Durante a negociação, um desconto foi concedido devido a uma avaria na traseira do carro, reduzindo o preço para R$ 68 mil. Após realizar o pagamento, parte do qual foi coberta por um empréstimo de R$ 30 mil, a vítima descobriu que o carro tinha placas clonadas e era roubado.

O caso foi registrado na delegacia, mas o vendedor falso desapareceu. Especialistas em trânsito destacam a importância da cautela ao comprar veículos usados, como realizar vistorias completas e verificar a documentação.

snippet.title: Why Is Ladder Line 450 Ohms — But Coax Is 50 Ohms?
snippet.description:
Why is coaxial cable commonly 50 ohms, while twin-lead, ladder line, and open-wire transmission lines can be 300, 450, or even 600 ohms?

In this video, we look at the physics that determines the characteristic impedance of a transmission line — and why there is no hidden 50-ohm or 450-ohm resistance inside the cable.

We’ll see how conductor spacing, conductor size, capacitance, inductance, and dielectric material determine characteristic impedance, and why increasing the spacing between conductors can produce transmission lines with much higher impedance.

We’ll also compare 50-ohm coax with 300-ohm twin-lead, 450-ohm ladder line, and 600-ohm open-wire line, and examine an important question:

Can a transmission line have a high SWR and still lose very little RF energy?

Using a dipole as an example, we’ll see why SWR alone does not tell you how much power is being lost, why low-loss balanced transmission line can operate efficiently with substantial SWR, and what an antenna tuner actually does when a 50-ohm transmitter is connected to a high-impedance transmission line.

Topics include:

• 50-ohm and 75-ohm coax
• 300-ohm twin-lead
• 450-ohm ladder line
• 600-ohm open-wire line
• Characteristic impedance
• Capacitance and inductance per unit length
• Conductor spacing and diameter
• SWR and reflected waves
• Transmission-line loss
• Dipole feed-point impedance
• Balanced vs. unbalanced transmission lines
• Antenna tuners and impedance transformation

If you enjoy clear explanations of RF, antennas, transmission lines, and amateur radio fundamentals, please subscribe to Telecom Training.

#hamradio #ts890s #HF #cw #antenna #horizontal #sota #operating #chasing #working #portable 

This is an operational video.  Some Patreon team members have requested more videos that cover real-world operation. Watch as I employ various techniques to chase SOTA (Summits On The Air) activators using CW mode.  I just happened to be using the Kenwood TS-890S at the time, but the techniques can apply to other transceivers.    

Most videos are released exclusively for the S7 (Executive) and S9 (VIP) members of my Patreon support team.  Without them, no videos would be released.  The S7 (Executive) members have access to many videos.  The S9 (VIP) members have access to all videos.  Plus S9 (VIP) members who subscribe annually have access to my written menu optimizations guides and FT8 configuration guides.  A few videos get released for public viewing, but the bulk of the premium content is for those who support this mission financially.

If you have been regularly watching my videos for the past few years, you know that I typically use Yaesu radios to teach operating techniques.  I also created a tutorial series for the FTdx10, FTdx101, and FT-710, and I’m periodically releasing tutorial videos for the Yaesu FTX-1 Optima.

Note that most of the operating techniques I show and teach on my channel can be applied to other transceivers, even other brands of transceivers.  Some knobs or buttons might be labeled differently but the function is the same.  I have no allegiance to Yaesu. No manufacturer makes a perfect radio. They all have strengths, and they all have weaknesses. I like to point those out.  I want my viewers to know the good, the bad, and the ugly, so they can make informed purchase decisions. snippet.title: The Hidden, Unrealized Benefit To Parks On The Air (POTA) - I Never Expected This!
snippet.description:
POTA gave me something I never really expected.

It gave me a reason to get out, explore new places and see things I probably never would have stopped to see otherwise.

In this video, I’m at Victoria Settlement Provincial Historic Site in Alberta, beside the North Saskatchewan River. It was the final Alberta stop on this part of my 2026 Cross Canada Adventure, and a perfect example of what portable ham radio has given me over the years.

I knew almost nothing about Victoria Settlement before I arrived. But because radio gave me a reason to go there, I spent time exploring the site, learning some of its history, seeing the aftermath of a recent storm and simply enjoying a quiet place along the river.

Then, of course, I played some radio.

Conditions during the Alberta trip had been difficult, but there were still some good contacts, including Finland, and one very tempting signal from Angola that I just couldn’t quite reach.

But what stayed with me from POTA goes well beyond the contacts.

It taught me to go somewhere new. Explore. Step outside my comfort zone. Spend time in nature. Slow down. Enjoy the quiet. Learn something about the places I visit.

Those are things I now carry with me wherever my ham radio adventures take me.

Sometimes portable ham radio gives you the reason to go.

What you discover along the way can become the best part of the journey.

snippet.title: REVIEW: XIEGU G7250 - LA NUEVA EMISORA QUE ROMPE PARADIGMAS
snippet.description:
https://www.todo-sdr.com/review-xiegu-g7250/
Enlace de compra: https://www.wimo.com/es/xiegu-g7250


🔥 ¡Hoy tenemos en Radio Búnker una de las radios más diferentes que ha presentado Xiegu!

En este vídeo hacemos una primera toma de contacto y pruebas con la nueva Xiegu G7250, una emisora HF + 6 metros multimodo que apuesta por un concepto muy particular: separar la unidad de control de la unidad PA mediante un cable de interconexión.

La G7250 ofrece 100 W desde 160 hasta 10 metros y 90 W en 6 metros, incorpora sintonizador de antena interno y dispone de dos conectores de antena. También encontramos conexión LAN, USB, control mediante pantalla táctil, espectro, cascada, filtros, reducción de ruido, memorias y múltiples funciones de configuración.

Pero una de las cosas que más me ha llamado la atención es la calidad de construcción. Tanto el panel de control como la unidad PA transmiten una sensación de producto mucho más cuidado de lo que podríamos esperar por su precio.

La unidad que aparece en este vídeo corresponde a una versión de preserie con firmware 1.0, por lo que algunas funciones y características podrían cambiar en futuras versiones.

En el momento de grabar este vídeo, el precio indicado para Europa es de 1090 €, con disponibilidad prevista para noviembre.
